opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a common assumption that if a big general-purpose model gets good enough to automate science, it will just keep absorbing every other task, and specialized systems become obsolete. I'm skeptical of that, for a few reasons.

First, look at what doing science well actually produces. It's not just a bag of facts. It's structured models: causal theories, simulators, physical laws, algorithms that are compact and have explicit assumptions. If an AI scientist succeeds, one of the first things it would do is build exactly those kinds of specialized tools, because they're dramatically more efficient and reliable than reasoning everything out in a giant neural network each time. Human science works this way already. We don't have one person who intuits protein structure, weather, and bridge loads. We build specialized instruments and models and then compose them. So I'd almost turn the question around: automating science is a path *toward* specialized systems, not away from them.

Second, there's efficiency. A monolithic model pays the full cost of a huge forward pass for every query, even when the problem has a known structure that a small, targeted program could solve exactly. A probabilistic program for a specific inference problem, or a planner with a well-specified model, can be orders of magnitude cheaper and also come with guarantees. When you care about cost, latency, or running at scale, that matters a lot.

Third, and this is the part I care most about, is reliability and accountability. With a specialized, structured system, you can inspect its assumptions, check where it's uncertain, verify its behavior in a given domain, and know when it's out of its depth. With a monolithic model, you're mostly relying on behavioral testing of a system whose internals you don't understand, and it generalizes in ways that are hard to predict. For high-stakes uses like medicine, infrastructure, and governance, I think people will rightly prefer systems whose scope is bounded and whose reasoning is legible.

And there's a safety angle too. A world of many specialized, composable tools, each with a clear purpose, is one where power is more distributed and it's easier to keep humans in the loop on what gets combined and how. That's a different trajectory from concentrating every capability inside one agent and hoping it's aligned.

So my view isn't that big general models are useless. They're very useful as glue, as interfaces, as hypothesis generators. But even in the world where they first crack automated science, I expect the frontier of actual performance on many tasks to move toward structured, specialized systems, partly because that's what good science tends to build.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to notice is that even if you accept the premise that a big general-purpose model is the thing that gets us to automated science first, that doesn't actually tell you what the end state looks like. Those are two different questions. One is, what's the fastest path to being able to do science without humans in the loop? And the other is, once you have that capability, what do you actually do with it?

And my claim is that one of the first things an automated scientist would do is figure out how to build better tools than itself. Because that's what science does. Historically, when we understand a domain well, we don't keep solving problems with raw human cognition. We build a calculator, we build a compiler, we build a chess engine. Those things are narrow, they're transparent in a way the general system isn't, and they're way more efficient per unit of compute. A monolithic model that's good at protein folding is still carrying around all this machinery for writing poetry and summarizing emails that it doesn't need for that task.

So if you're an automated scientist and you care about efficiency, reliability, verifiability, you're going to specialize. You're going to say, here's a well-understood problem, let's distill it into something small and checkable and fast. And then the general system becomes more like an orchestrator or a researcher that spins up specialists, rather than being the thing that does every task end-to-end.

There's also a safety and trust angle here that I think matters a lot. A specialized system has a scope. You can characterize what it does, you can test it against a spec, you can audit it. With a monolith, you're always asking, what else might this thing do? And I think any serious scientific civilization, human or automated, is going to prefer tools it can actually reason about over tools that are impressive but opaque.

So I'd put it like this: general models might be how we get there, but specialization is what competent engineering looks like once you've arrived. The monolith is the scaffolding, not the building.

astra-6.text:
I think automating science might actually accelerate the development of specialized systems. Even if a monolithic model gets us there first, one of the things it can do as a scientist is investigate better architectures, better learning algorithms, and better ways to divide up a problem.

For a particular task, a specialized system can exploit structure that a general-purpose model has to learn implicitly. You might have a simulator for predicting physical dynamics, a planner for searching over possible actions, and a language model for interpreting what someone wants. Those components can have different strengths, and you can allocate computation where it’s most useful.

Of course, there’s a cost to coordinating them. Specialization doesn’t automatically win. But being the first system capable of automating science doesn’t mean you’re the most efficient architecture for every scientific problem—or even for doing science overall. You could be the system that discovers the more specialized systems that eventually outperform you.

sol-6.1.text:
I think automating science actually gives you a mechanism for producing systems that outperform the system doing the science. Being a great scientist doesn’t mean that you can personally do everything better than the tools you invent. You can design a calculator that’s better than you at arithmetic, or an algorithm that solves a particular problem much more efficiently than your own reasoning process does.

So even if a monolithic model gets us to the point where we can automate scientific research, that research can discover better architectures, better training procedures, and specialized algorithms for different domains. The resulting systems might be much cheaper, more reliable, or more capable on those tasks than repeatedly asking the general model to reason through them.

The question then becomes how you compose those capabilities. You might still have a general system coordinating things, but much of the actual work could happen in specialized components. So I don’t see success at automating science as establishing that a monolithic architecture is the endpoint. It could be precisely what allows us to discover something better.
